bigPicture: Iran said three more oil tankers hit its mines in the Strait of Hormuz and sent drones at a US radar in Bahrain, while Saudi Arabia shot down Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh, keeping the Gulf war at the centre of the world's energy worries before oil markets reopen on Monday. Ukraine's president said US negotiators had, for the first time, asked whether Kyiv would give up Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, and the Kremlin confirmed that Putin, Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen on 19 November. In the US, thousands more flights were cancelled after Friday's nationwide ground stop, and measles deaths reached 10 on state counts. Across Europe, people marched over living costs in France and housing in Portugal, while bitcoin slid to a three-month low on bets of a US rate rise. Stock markets were closed for the weekend, so the market figures are Friday's closing levels.

CEO Nicolas Bos said demand in China remains weak, finanzen.ch reported; the SMI fell 0.3% to 15,106. A Saturday ad-hoc-news report recalled Reuters reporting that Richemont is among firms in talks to join a consortium for a De Beers stake, with no binding deal.
companies.name: Richemont

watchFor: Demand in China, where management expects a recovery but cannot say when (finanzen.ch)
The company's expectation of a volatile economic and geopolitical environment (finanzen.ch)
Talks on joining the De Beers consortium, reported by Reuters (via ad-hoc-news)

stocks.overview: Weekend news moved several companies onto the desk ahead of Monday's open: Meta was fined €805 million by Italy's privacy regulator and Reuters reported it will appeal; L3Harris was named by the US Transportation Secretary as the contractor whose router work preceded Friday's nationwide flight halt, and airlines such as United and Delta cancelled about a quarter of Saturday's flights; Expedia faces a hacker group's claim of hundreds of millions of stolen records. Strategy's bitcoin holdings lost value as bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on Sunday, and Saudi Aramco is in focus after Saudi Arabia said it destroyed Houthi missiles fired at Riyadh. Friday's closes still reflect the chip sell-off (Nvidia −2.0%, AMD −8.8%) before Nvidia's results on Tuesday 17 November, while in Warsaw Allegro led the WIG20 for a second day.

stories.everyday: Higher shipping and insurance costs for oil, gas and fertiliser eventually show up in prices at the petrol station and in food. Poland, like most of Europe, relies on imported oil, so it is exposed to any jump in crude prices.
stories.rankWhy: The strait is the main exit for Gulf oil and gas, so any new danger there affects fuel prices, shipping costs and inflation worldwide.
stories.title: Iran says three oil tankers hit its mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz; the UN says at least 25 seafarers have died there since February
stories.what: Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said on Saturday that two oil tankers, one of them a supertanker, exploded and caught fire after hitting a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran's regular navy said a third tanker east of the strait was forced to stop after striking a mine. Iran said the ships had switched off their tracking systems and used routes it has not authorised; it gave no names, flags or casualty figures, and none of the incidents has been independently confirmed (AFP via The Manila Times). The US military says it has cleared the main routes of mines and that the waterway is open. At the UN Security Council on Friday, UN assistant secretary-general Khaled Khiari said at least 25 seafarers have been killed in and around the strait since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February; the International Maritime Organization (IMO, the UN shipping agency) counted 136 security incidents from 1 March to 11 November, and the UK agency UKMTO says traffic is about 65% below pre-war levels (Al Jazeera).
stories.why: Since the war began, Iran demands that ships get its permission to cross the strait and attacks those that do not, while the US blockades Iranian ports and escorts tankers (AFP). Each reported mine strike raises the risk that shipowners avoid the route and that insurers charge more, which the UN's Khiari said is pushing up energy, transport and insurance costs, feeding inflation and limiting fertiliser shipments. Oil markets were closed at the weekend, so the first price reaction comes when trading resumes.

stories.everyday: Gulf tensions keep a 'risk premium' in oil prices, which affects fuel costs everywhere. Travellers to the Gulf may face airspace warnings or flight changes.
stories.rankWhy: A direct Iranian attack on US forces in a Gulf state risks widening the war around the world's most important oil route.
stories.title: Iran says six drones attacked a US radar at a base in Bahrain; Bahrain says it shot down an Iranian drone and tells residents to take shelter
stories.what: Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said on Sunday that six drones targeted a US air-defence radar at the Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, calling it the 'second phase' of a response to US actions; it gave no evidence of damage (Kurdistan24). Bahrain's military said its air defences intercepted several Iranian projectiles early on Sunday, and Bahrain issued two nationwide threat alerts, its first since September, urging people to move to the nearest safe place (AP via WRAL; Kurdistan24). On Friday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it shot down two Iranian drones heading for Bahrain and denied Iran's claim that a US early-warning radar was destroyed (Business Recorder, AFP). The IRGC also claimed it shot down a US MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island on Saturday; the US has not confirmed any drone loss.
stories.why: The IRGC says the strikes answer a US attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran's Hormozgan province, which CENTCOM has not commented on (Kurdistan24). Reuters reported that Friday's claim was Iran's first claim of an attack on US military assets in a Gulf state since early September, so a second wave suggests a renewed cycle of tit-for-tat attacks even as Qatar mediates between Washington and Tehran.

stories.everyday: Poland is part of the European negotiating team, so the talks directly concern its security. An end to the war could, over time, lower energy and defence risks in the region, but no deal is close.
stories.rankWhy: Any deal trading territory for alliance membership would reshape European security, Ukraine's future and the risks priced into European markets.
stories.title: Zelensky says US negotiators asked, for the first time, whether Ukraine would leave Donbas in exchange for NATO membership
stories.what: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said US negotiators raised, for the first time in the talks, the idea of Ukraine withdrawing from Donbas (the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, which Russia partly occupies) in return for joining NATO, and said this puts NATO 'back on the agenda' (Reuters via ABC News). He said Kyiv is not ready to give up territory and would put a deal to a national referendum only if it included security guarantees, a strong, well-funded army and money for reconstruction. He also rejected Vladimir Putin's offer of a local humanitarian ceasefire in the frontline city of Kostiantynivka. US-brokered Ukraine–Russia talks in Abu Dhabi ended on Wednesday without a breakthrough apart from an agreed exchange of more than 1,000 prisoners; no official US or Kremlin response to his account was reported.
stories.why: Putin has long called Ukrainian NATO membership a red line and cited it as a reason for the 2022 invasion, so the idea faces strong Russian opposition (ABC/Reuters). For Ukraine, NATO's mutual-defence clause would be the strongest possible guarantee against a new attack, which is why Kyiv links any concession to such guarantees. EU leaders agreed in Dublin that Europe's negotiating team will include the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland plus EU officials, and Zelensky said the US told him Europe will have a seat at upcoming talks.

stories.everyday: No direct effect yet. Progress on arms control or the wars could calm markets and energy prices; a failure could do the opposite.
stories.rankWhy: A meeting of the leaders of the world's three biggest military powers could affect arms control, the Iran war and Ukraine.
stories.title: The Kremlin confirms Putin, Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen on 19 November, on the sidelines of the APEC summit
stories.what: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the state news agency TASS on Saturday that Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will hold a three-way meeting on 19 November in Shenzhen, China, during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on 18–19 November (Anadolu). Trump said on 8 November that he expected to meet both leaders there, and China's Foreign Ministry said on 6 November that discussions were under way. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said Russia and the US have not agreed a separate Putin–Trump meeting on the sidelines.
stories.why: The White House had already announced the plan (covered in the previous edition); Russia's confirmation makes it more likely to happen. A three-way format is unusual: the US and Russia hold most of the world's nuclear warheads and China is expanding its arsenal, so any talks on arms limits or on the wars in Ukraine and Iran would matter far beyond the three countries.

stories.everyday: Anyone flying to or within the US this weekend may face cancellations; knock-on delays can affect connecting flights from Europe. Airlines face extra costs for rebooking and compensation.
stories.rankWhy: The longest nationwide halt to US flights since 9/11 stranded hundreds of thousands of travellers and exposed weaknesses in air-traffic control infrastructure.
stories.title: US airlines cancel more than 6,400 flights on Saturday after Friday's nationwide ground stop; officials trace the fault to new routers installed by contractor L3Harris
stories.what: About 9,200 US flights were cancelled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted nearly all departures for almost five hours; by 9:35 p.m. US Eastern time on Saturday more than 6,400 flights had been cancelled and 8,000 delayed, and 875 Sunday flights were already cancelled, according to FlightAware data cited by Reuters. Delta, United and American each cancelled about a quarter of Saturday's flights and JetBlue nearly 45%. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said 17 of the FAA's 22 en-route control centres were affected but 'nothing was fully lost', and expected operations to be largely normal by late Sunday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem was traced to contractor L3Harris installing at least one new router at a remote facility, and that it is not yet known whether it was user error, installer error or a faulty router; Polish broadcaster TVN24 reported that he preliminarily ruled out a cyberattack.
stories.why: Duffy said the faulty equipment made 'over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds', disrupting communication with planes and radar (Reuters via Business Recorder). He is now asking Congress for $50 billion to upgrade air-traffic control, up from $30 billion; incoming House Democratic committee leaders said only $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved last year has been spent.

stories.everyday: Southeast Asia makes many electronics, clothes and shoes sold in Europe, so energy shortages or trade shifts there can affect supply and prices of consumer goods.
stories.rankWhy: The 11-member bloc of nearly 694 million people is among the regions hit hardest by oil and gas shortages from the Iran war.
stories.title: ASEAN leaders open their summit in Manila with the Middle East energy shock, Myanmar's war and the South China Sea at the top of the agenda
stories.what: Southeast Asian leaders opened the ASEAN summit in Manila on Sunday; it runs from 15 to 17 November (Al Jazeera, AP). AP reported that Donald Trump is expected to land in Manila on Tuesday 17 November for a Quad meeting (US, Japan, Australia, India) and a special summit with ASEAN leaders, and to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday before flying to Shenzhen for APEC. India's Narendra Modi, Canada's Mark Carney, Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov are also attending. Al Jazeera reports that the Philippines declared a national energy emergency in March and that ASEAN countries have faced US tariff increases of 10 to 12.5 percent. Talks with China on a South China Sea 'code of conduct', under way since 2005, are not expected to be concluded at this summit, analysts told Al Jazeera.
stories.why: Southeast Asian economies depend heavily on imported Gulf oil and gas, so the disruption in Hormuz has caused shortages and price spikes there; leaders want a common response, including a shared regional oil stockpile that is still under study. US tariffs have pushed the bloc to deepen trade ties with other partners such as Canada, which has concluded free-trade talks with the Philippines.

stories.everyday: Attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure add to the risk premium in oil prices. For Yemenis, displacement means loss of homes, income and access to food and health care.
stories.rankWhy: Renewed war in Yemen threatens Saudi oil facilities and is displacing hundreds of thousands in one of the world's poorest countries.
stories.title: Saudi Arabia says it destroyed two Houthi ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh as Yemen's war spreads; the UN says 340,000 people have fled their homes since August
stories.what: The Saudi-led coalition said early on Sunday that its air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthis towards Riyadh and shot down drones over the Eastern Region; no damage was reported (Al Jazeera, AP). Saudi authorities say at least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since 23 September, and the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday. Houthi health officials said an airstrike on Sanaa wounded two women and two children and blamed Saudi Arabia, which did not comment (AP). The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that more than 340,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since August (Middle East Monitor, Al Jazeera).
stories.why: The Houthis are an Iran-allied rebel group fighting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which Saudi-led forces support (Al Jazeera). The government launched an offensive called 'Dawn of Yemen' on 5 October aiming to retake the capital Sanaa, ending a period of relative calm that began in April 2022, Middle East Monitor reported. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh's airport and the East-West oil pipeline, which matters because that pipeline lets Saudi oil bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.everyday: Winter rain and cold worsen conditions in tent camps: Al Jazeera reports cold-related deaths have risen to 11. Aid agencies, including those funded by EU taxpayers, face growing needs.
stories.rankWhy: Escalating strikes strain the Gaza ceasefire and the humanitarian situation of about two million people as winter sets in.
stories.title: Israel kills Hamas's Rafah commander in a strike on a tent area in Khan Younis; 17–18 Muslim-majority countries condemn an earlier strike on Gaza's Nasser hospital
stories.what: Israel's military and the Shin Bet security agency said an airstrike in southern Gaza killed Samir Abu Younis, commander of Hamas's Rafah brigade; Hamas confirmed his death (AP via WRAL). Al Jazeera reported that the drone strike hit a tent sheltering displaced people in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, wounding two others. Gaza's Health Ministry said on Saturday that 16 people had been killed in the previous 48 hours and at least 1,643 since the ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. A joint statement issued by Pakistan on Saturday and backed by foreign ministers of 17 countries, according to Dawn (Anadolu counts 18, so sources differ), condemned in the 'strongest terms' an Israeli strike on the surgery ward of Nasser Hospital early on Thursday, which Dawn reported killed at least six people, including a 13-year-old boy.
stories.why: The countries said attacks on medical facilities violate international humanitarian law, which protects hospitals and medical workers, and asked the US and the 'Board of Peace' overseeing the ceasefire to press Israel to comply and lift aid restrictions (Dawn). Israel says it targets militants; Gaza's Health Ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not separate civilians from fighters in its figures.

stories.everyday: People holding crypto have lost a large part of its value in a week. Crypto is not protected like a bank deposit, which is why regulators warn it is very risky.
stories.rankWhy: A sharp fall in the biggest cryptocurrency affects millions of small investors and is a signal of falling appetite for risk before Monday's stock-market open.
stories.title: Bitcoin falls to a three-month low near $62,000, down about 15% in a week, as bets on a US rate rise and fund outflows hit crypto
stories.what: Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on Sunday, a three-month low, and traded near $64,500 at the time of crypto.news's report, down about 4.3% in 24 hours and nearly 15% in seven days; unlike stock exchanges, crypto markets trade at weekends. US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) saw about $1.91 billion of net withdrawals over seven sessions from 5 to 13 November, according to Farside Investors data cited by crypto.news. Data firm CoinGlass counted about $1.96 billion of crypto liquidations in 24 hours, roughly $750 million of them in bitcoin, mostly bets on rising prices.
stories.why: Crypto.news linked the slide to ETF outflows, forced selling of leveraged positions and inflation worries: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, keeping attention on whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates. Higher interest rates make assets that pay no income, like bitcoin and gold, less attractive, and a 'liquidation' happens when a trader who borrowed to bet on prices is forced to sell as prices fall, which pushes prices down further.

stories.everyday: Strikes can disrupt transport and schools in France, including for travellers from Poland. The debate shows how the cost of living is driving political tension across Europe.
stories.rankWhy: A fifth straight weekend of protests and new strikes add pressure on the French government in the euro area's second-largest economy.
stories.title: More than 100,000 march across France over living costs and a bill giving police more legal protection, says the Interior Ministry
stories.what: France's Interior Ministry said about 106,000 people joined Saturday's protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris, the lowest weekend turnout in recent weeks; student unions put turnout at 200,000, including almost 100,000 in Paris (TRT World). Marchers protested against rising living costs and inequality, a bill that would presume police officers acted in self-defence when they used their weapons, and for better learning conditions and children's rights. It was the fifth consecutive Saturday of protests after more than a month of high-school blockades; on Thursday a union-led strike drew more than 500,000 people on official figures.
stories.why: Supporters of the police bill, including Marine Le Pen's party, say officers should not automatically be suspected of excessive force, while activists say it would hinder investigations into police brutality (TRT World). Unions reject the government's offer to raise the minimum wage by 0.6% as 'crumbs' and have called new strikes for Tuesday.

stories.everyday: Housing affordability is a political issue in Poland too, so the Portuguese debate over rent caps and new building is worth watching.
stories.rankWhy: Housing costs are one of Europe's biggest social issues, and Portugal shows the EU's steepest rise in prices relative to incomes.
stories.title: Tens of thousands march in more than 30 Portuguese cities and towns against soaring home prices and rents
stories.what: Large crowds marched on Saturday in more than 30 cities and towns in Portugal in what AP called the biggest protest yet over housing costs; riot police with dogs broke up some demonstrations, and critics accused them of heavy-handed tactics (AP via WRAL; Anadolu counts 32 cities). Protesters demanded caps on rent increases, stronger protection against eviction and more affordable homes. Eurostat figures cited by AP show Portugal's house price-to-income ratio rose 61% from 2015 to 2025, the largest increase in the EU, ahead of the Netherlands at 34%.
stories.why: Portugal's statistics office INE reported house prices up almost 20% between the first quarters of 2025 and 2026, and the government says rents have risen 68% since 2020 (AP). When prices rise much faster than wages, young people and lower-income families are pushed out of cities or into overcrowded housing.

stories.everyday: Measles also circulates in Europe. Measles vaccination is part of Poland's childhood vaccination schedule; two doses give the protection described above.
stories.rankWhy: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases, and falling vaccination in the world's largest economy is a warning for public health everywhere.
stories.title: US measles deaths reach 10 this year on state counts, while the CDC's official tally is six, as the country loses its measles-free status
stories.what: States have reported 10 measles-associated deaths in the US this year, seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin and one in New York; Wisconsin reported an infant's death on Friday (Al Jazeera). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the federal health agency, counts six; Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked CDC director Erica Schwartz not to count the others, saying there was no evidence they were measles-associated, and the CDC says it is working on a standard definition. The US has more than 5,400 confirmed cases this year, more than double the 2,289 in 2025, and the Pan American Health Organization revoked its measles-free status after more than 12 months of uninterrupted transmission.
stories.why: Kindergarten vaccination coverage fell from 95.2% in 2019–20 to 92.4% in 2025–26, Al Jazeera reported; two doses of the MMR vaccine give about 97% protection. Because measles spreads so easily, outbreaks take hold when coverage drops below the level needed for herd immunity (about 95% is the commonly cited target).

stories.everyday: Expedia customers, including in Poland, should watch for phishing emails using their booking details and change reused passwords.
stories.rankWhy: One of the world's biggest travel companies may have exposed data on hundreds of millions of customers, raising risks of fraud and phishing.
stories.title: Hacker group claims data on nearly a billion Expedia traveller records after Expedia confirms a breach through an outside vendor
stories.what: A Russian extortion group called n0n, active since mid-September, claims it stole more than 830 million loyalty-programme records, 58 million traveller profiles and over 333 million account and credential records from Expedia, Security Affairs reported on Saturday; the figures are unverified. Expedia confirmed on 12 November that attackers reached its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider in a supply-chain attack that also hit other companies; it has not confirmed the group's figures and says its investigation continues and its platforms remain safe. Security Affairs reported that researchers at Wiz and Sentra link it to a stolen access key from Qubole, a former Expedia vendor, but Skift reported that Expedia has not confirmed any link and the researchers have not publicly named Expedia as affected, so sources differ.
stories.why: In a supply-chain attack, criminals break into a supplier that a company trusts and use that access to reach the company's own systems (Security Affairs). Groups like n0n steal data and threaten to publish it unless paid, rather than locking systems with ransomware.

stories.everyday: It shows that EU rules give people in Poland, too, the right to refuse apps access to their photos; checking app permissions on a phone is worthwhile.
stories.rankWhy: One of the largest European privacy fines against a tech giant sets a precedent for how apps may access data on people's phones.
stories.title: Italy's privacy regulator fines Meta €805 million for letting the Facebook app access Android users' photos without proper consent
stories.what: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta €805 million, roughly 0.47% of its global turnover, after finding that the Facebook Android app accessed photos, videos and their metadata on about 20 million Italian users' phones without specific consent or proper notice, The Next Web reported on 14 November, citing Reuters. The access supported a feature, available since 2023, that suggests phone photos as post ideas. Meta must, within 60 days, ask for separate consent for the feature and keep it off by default; Reuters later reported that Meta called the fine disproportionate and will appeal.
stories.why: The Garante acted under ePrivacy rules (Article 122 of Italy's privacy code), which require informed consent before an app accesses data stored on a device, rather than under the GDPR; because ePrivacy has no 'one-stop-shop', Italy could act instead of Ireland's regulator, which usually leads on Meta, The Next Web explained. Meta argued the case belonged in Ireland.

stories.everyday: Cheaper launches mean more satellites for internet, navigation and Earth observation, services many people use daily without noticing.
stories.rankWhy: Reusing the whole rocket could sharply cut the cost of launching satellites and future Moon and Mars missions.
stories.title: SpaceX catches a Starship upper stage with its launch tower for the first time after a flight to orbit
stories.what: SpaceX caught Ship 42, the upper stage of its Starship rocket, with the robotic arms of its launch tower at Starbase in Texas at 4:20 p.m. US Eastern time (22:20 Warsaw) on 14 November, about 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off on Friday evening, Space.com reported. It was the first time a Starship upper stage returning from orbit was caught; SpaceX had previously caught the Super Heavy booster on three flights, but this time the booster was diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico after a low-fuel alarm. The ship also deployed 26 Starlink satellites.
stories.why: Catching a stage lets SpaceX inspect, refuel and fly it again quickly instead of building a new one, which is how reusability lowers launch costs (Space.com). The upper stage is harder to catch than the booster because it comes back from orbit at far higher speed; SpaceX plans to try catching both stages on a future flight.

stories.everyday: A Congress controlled by the opposition party can block or reshape the president's plans, including on tariffs and spending, which affects the dollar and global markets.
stories.rankWhy: The final count decides how large the new Democratic majorities in Congress will be, which shapes US budgets, investigations and policy.
stories.title: Democrat Mary Peltola widens her lead in Alaska's Senate race, and Lauren Boebert loses her Colorado House seat, as US midterm counting continues
stories.what: With about 96% of ballots counted, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 10,412 votes, with 49.84% to his 46.09%, Anadolu reported; if no candidate reaches 50%, a ranked-choice tabulation will be held on 18 November. In Colorado's 4th district, Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, defeated Republican Representative Lauren Boebert by 48.8% to 47.9% with about 99% counted, in a district Donald Trump won by more than 18 points in 2024. Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the 3 November midterms and take control when the new Congress convenes on 3 January 2027; several House races remain undecided.
stories.why: Anadolu reported that a Peltola win would give Democrats 56 of 100 Senate seats and make her the first Indigenous Alaskan elected to the Senate. Under ranked-choice voting, voters rank candidates; if nobody wins a majority of first choices, the last-placed candidates are eliminated and their votes passed to voters' next choices until someone has a majority.

stories.everyday: Sudan is one of the world's largest humanitarian crises; refugees have fled to Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, and some reach Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Control of Kordofan's farmland, gold and oil fields could shift the course of a war that has displaced over 14 million people.
stories.title: Sudan's army pushes west through Kordofan as a local group says RSF fighters killed 10 civilians in Al-Nuhud
stories.what: Sudan's army (SAF) and allied forces took control of several villages and localities in West Kordofan, including the town of al-Khuwai, on Friday, Al Jazeera reported; the offensive has broken the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces' (RSF) siege of El-Obeid, capital of North Kordofan. A local relief group said RSF fighters killed 10 civilians in Al-Nuhud in West Kordofan since Thursday, Anadolu reported; the RSF still holds Al-Nuhud and all five Darfur states. Al Jazeera puts the war's death toll at about 150,000 and the displaced at more than 14 million of Sudan's 53 million people.
stories.why: Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera say the RSF has shifted from attack to defence and may pull back to Darfur, and that Kordofan matters for its agriculture, gold and oil: the Heglig and Balila fields in West Kordofan produce 90% of Sudan's oil, and South Sudan's oil exports pass through Sudanese territory.

stories.everyday: EU climate policy, including carbon prices that affect electricity and heating bills in Poland, is shaped partly by what is agreed at these summits.
stories.rankWhy: The talks set the direction of global climate policy, which affects energy prices, investment and countries most exposed to climate damage.
stories.title: COP31 climate talks in Antalya end their first week split over fossil fuels and adaptation money, with five days left
stories.what: The UN climate summit COP31 opened on 9 November in Antalya, Türkiye, and is scheduled to close on 20 November; Türkiye's Murat Kurum is COP31 president and Australia chairs the negotiations, The Rio Times reported. At the end of week one, the Arab Group, including Saudi Arabia, opposed references in any decision to Brazil's voluntary roadmaps for moving away from fossil fuels and halting deforestation, and the African Group's request for a separate agenda item on tripling adaptation finance was left off. The US government is skipping the talks for a second year; a group of 19 Democratic members of Congress is attending. On Saturday UN climate chief Simon Stiell urged negotiators to move quickly to the hardest issues and avoid tactical delays, and Australia's Chris Bowen expects a first draft of the deal early next week (Reuters via WMBD).
stories.why: Adaptation finance pays for defences against climate damage, such as flood barriers, and poorer countries say rich countries have not delivered enough (The Rio Times). Under the 2024 COP29 deal, developed countries lead on mobilising at least $300 billion a year by 2035. Big fossil-fuel producers resist firm commitments because their economies depend on oil and gas revenue.

stories.everyday: If Stola is right, such incidents aim to stir hostility between Poles, Ukrainians and Jews; the investigation should show who was behind them.
stories.rankWhy: Vandalism that inflames Polish–Ukrainian and Polish–Jewish relations fits a pattern of suspected hybrid operations against Poland.
stories.title: 'Slava UPA' painted on two Warsaw monuments, including the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes; a historian suspects a Russian-inspired provocation
stories.what: Red inscriptions reading 'Slava UPA' (glory to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a World War II nationalist group responsible for massacres of Poles) appeared on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes in Warsaw's Muranów district and on a nearby monument to soldiers of the 1st Polish Army, WP and TVN24 reported on Saturday. Warsaw police received two reports and are investigating, a police spokesman told TVN24. Historian Dariusz Stola, a former director of the POLIN museum, said the act fits a pattern of hostile hybrid operations, most likely with Russian inspiration and money; police have not announced any finding on who did it.
stories.why: Hybrid operations combine sabotage, vandalism and disinformation to divide societies without open war; Stola cited similar cases in other cities and online offers of $500 for such acts, but his attribution to Russia is his own view. WP reported a separate case in which Gdańsk prosecutors charged a 17-year-old Ukrainian citizen over hateful inscriptions on seven monuments.

stories.everyday: Continued strikes keep security risks high on the EU's eastern border, right next to Poland, and damage to Ukraine's grid makes its winter harder for millions.
stories.rankWhy: Daily strikes on Ukraine's cities and power grid continue even as peace talks go on, keeping pressure on civilians and energy supplies before winter.
stories.title: Russia launches 132 drones at Ukraine overnight, with hits at 20 locations, as cross-border strikes kill people on both sides
stories.what: Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 132 drones overnight into Sunday, including 78 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, and that 106 were shot down or suppressed by 08:00, with hits recorded at 20 locations; it did not name them, and no casualty figures were given (UNN; 112.ua). On Saturday, officials on both sides reported at least five people killed: Russia's Belgorod region said a Ukrainian drone killed a couple and their daughter in Proletarsky, while Ukrainian officials reported one woman killed in the Donetsk region and one person killed in the Kharkiv region (Anadolu via A News). A Russian strike on a power facility in the Odesa region on Saturday morning left nearly 50,000 people without electricity, the regional head said.
stories.why: Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter, and Ukraine has hit targets inside Russia with long-range drones; neither side's claims can be independently verified. The strikes continue alongside US-brokered talks, which Zelensky said Putin is not supporting with a ceasefire (ABC/Reuters).

stories.everyday: A firmer dollar makes fuel and many imported goods priced in dollars more expensive for Polish consumers and companies; people with dollar costs (travel, online purchases) pay more in złoty.
stories.rankWhy: A stronger dollar makes dollar-priced oil and dollar debts more expensive for the rest of the world, including Poland.
stories.title: The dollar ends its best week in two months at the highest since April 2025, pushing the euro and the yen lower
stories.what: The dollar index (DXY), which measures the dollar against six major currencies, closed Friday at 103.38, its highest since April 2025, after rising about 1% on the week, its best week in two months, Investrade reported. The euro fell to its lowest against the dollar since April 2025 and ended near $1.1022, and the yen briefly tested 160 per dollar before strengthening after Japan's finance minister said the government would respond appropriately to currency volatility. In Poland, the NBP's average dollar rate rose to 3.9852 złoty on Friday from 3.9676 on Thursday.
stories.why: Investrade attributed the dollar's rise to expectations of higher US interest rates after hot inflation data and hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials: when US rates are expected to rise, holding dollars pays more, so investors buy them. Markets price about an 88% chance of a quarter-point Fed rate rise in December.

stories.everyday: Low risk for most people in Europe; vaccines exist for people at higher risk.
stories.rankWhy: Mpox remains a global health concern, and rising cases in a country of 214 million are worth watching.
terms: Public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC)
stories.title: Brazil records its first mpox death of 2026 as cases in Rio de Janeiro double; officials say it is not an outbreak
stories.what: Brazil recorded its first mpox death of 2026 in Rio de Janeiro, the public health institute Fiocruz reported, according to AFP via Philstar. Brazil has 1,009 confirmed infections this year, mostly in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, and cases in Rio from September to November doubled compared with the rest of the year. Officials are not treating it as an outbreak, saying numbers are far below the 2022 peak; surveillance has been stepped up and 25,000 vaccine doses bought.
stories.why: Mpox is a viral disease spread mainly through close contact; the WHO declared it a public health emergency of international concern in 2022 and again in 2024 (Philstar/AFP).

stories.everyday: El Niño can also affect world prices of crops like coffee, cocoa and rice, which reach shoppers in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: El Niño-linked rains are hitting Ecuador's coast, a sign of the weather swings the climate pattern can bring.
stories.title: Heavy El Niño rains kill two in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city, and two people are missing
stories.what: Heavy rain on Friday flooded about 50 sectors of Guayaquil, and Infrastructure Minister Roberto Luque said two people died: a taxi driver who had a heart attack in his flooded car and a 17-year-old swept into a channel, whose body was found on Saturday, Infobae reported. Two more people were missing after falling into a canal, and rivers overflowed in Milagro and two other coastal provinces. Since the government declared a red alert on 28 August, El Niño has caused 12 other deaths and affected 26,786 people.
stories.why: El Niño is a periodic warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific that shifts rainfall patterns, typically bringing heavy rain to Ecuador's and Peru's coasts.

stories.everyday: The pope's messages reach Catholics worldwide, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The pope, who served for years in Peru, is using his trip to draw attention to crime and instability there.
stories.title: Pope Leo XIV laments the 'darkness' of violence in Peru as he visits his former diocese
stories.what: On the ninth day of a 12-day South America trip, Pope Leo XIV led a ceremony on Saturday at the cathedral in Chiclayo, where he was bishop from 2014 to 2023, and flew to the Andean community of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, AP reported. He prayed for an end to violence and urged peaceful change; he meets Amazonian and Indigenous peoples on Sunday and celebrates a final Mass in Lima on Monday. AP cited official data showing Peru's homicide rate nearly doubled in five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people, and extortion reports rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025.
stories.why: AP linked the pope's words to rising crime, extortion by criminal gangs and political instability in Peru.

stories.everyday: Poland's security depends on how the war ends; decisions in Berlin affect European defence spending and support for Ukraine.
stories.rankWhy: The meeting coordinates European security guarantees for Ukraine as US-led peace talks continue.
stories.title: Germany's Merz will host the 'Coalition of the Willing' on Ukraine in Berlin on Thursday
stories.what: Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham have invited the 'Coalition of the Willing', the countries ready to support Ukraine's security after a ceasefire, to the Federal Chancellery in Berlin on Thursday 19 November, the German government's deutschland.de reported. The agenda covers coordinating diplomatic efforts, security guarantees for Ukraine after the war and further support.
stories.why: European leaders want to make sure any peace deal includes credible guarantees so Russia cannot attack again, which is also the condition Zelensky set for any territorial deal.

stories.everyday: Travellers flying via high-altitude hubs with heart or lung conditions should ask a doctor first.
stories.rankWhy: Addis Ababa's Bole airport is one of Africa's biggest transit hubs, used by millions of travellers.
stories.title: Nigeria warns citizens with health problems about transiting Addis Ababa's high-altitude airport after 16 Nigerians died there this year
stories.what: Nigeria's foreign ministry said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa and urged people with heart or breathing conditions to get medical advice before travelling through Bole International Airport, KBC reported. It did not identify the travellers or causes of death and said it did not want to discourage travel via the city, which lies at 2,334 metres above sea level. No Ethiopian response was reported.
stories.why: At high altitude the air contains less oxygen per breath, which can strain people with cardiovascular or respiratory illness.

stories.everyday: No direct effect on Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The case concerns one of the deadliest attacks on Christians in Jordan in years and the country's use of the death penalty.
stories.title: Jordan's State Security Court sentences three men to death over the October attack on a church funeral that killed nine
stories.what: Jordan's State Security Court sentenced two brothers and their brother-in-law to death by hanging for the 23 October attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate, in which nine people were killed and about 25 wounded, Al Jazeera reported on Sunday. They were convicted of terrorist acts resulting in death, weapons offences, conspiracy and promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation. AP reported that authorities described them as extremists not tied to an organised group.
stories.why: The court tried the case as terrorism; such attacks on religious gatherings are rare in Jordan, which makes the case closely watched there.

stories.everyday: No direct effect on Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Militant violence in Pakistan's border regions affects the security of a large, nuclear-armed country.
stories.title: Pakistan's military says it killed 24 militants in operations in North Waziristan and Balochistan
stories.what: Pakistani security forces killed 24 people the military called 'terrorists' in operations in North Waziristan and Balochistan, and soldiers died in separate clashes, according to the military's media wing ISPR, Anadolu reported. The figures come from the military and could not be independently verified.
stories.why: Pakistan has faced rising attacks by militant groups in its north-west and in Balochistan, where separatists target security forces and infrastructure.

stories.everyday: Disappointing for fans.
stories.rankWhy: A sports result that matters to fans but has no measurable wider effect.
stories.title: Poland lose 1–2 to Romania in the Nations League in Bucharest; Lewandowski calls the goals conceded 'too easy'
stories.what: Poland lost 1–2 to Romania in Bucharest on Saturday 14 November in the UEFA Nations League, conceding two goals within four minutes, TVN24 reported. Captain Robert Lewandowski said the goals were too easy, and coach Jan Urban said he will not resign on his own; Poland have lost four away matches in 2026. UEFA approved a minute of silence for the victims of the Kraków attack before the next match against Sweden.
stories.why: The defeat puts pressure on the coach and the team's place in its group.

stories.everyday: Drivers should take care; fog can delay flights.
stories.rankWhy: Local weather warnings with limited impact.
stories.title: IMGW warns of strong wind in Poland's south-west on Sunday after a night of dense fog
stories.what: Poland's weather service IMGW issued first-degree (lowest-level) warnings for dense fog from 21:00 Saturday to 08:00 Sunday in parts of seven voivodeships, including counties around Warsaw, and for strong wind with gusts up to 80 km/h in parts of Lower Silesia and Opole from 04:00 to 16:00 on Sunday, TVN24 Meteo reported.
stories.why: Autumn high-pressure weather often brings fog; low-pressure systems bring wind.

stories.everyday: Eurovision fans in Poland can follow the new Asian edition.
stories.rankWhy: A new cultural event with little measurable wider effect.
stories.title: The Philippines wins the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok
stories.what: The Philippines won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok; 19-year-old Carmelle, the youngest contestant, won with 'Sobra-Sobra' and 211 points (93 from juries, 118 from viewers), according to the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), Anadolu reported.
stories.why: The EBU, which runs Eurovision, is expanding the format beyond Europe.

stories.everyday: Of interest to football fans.
stories.rankWhy: A sports result with no wider effect.
stories.title: Denmark beat Portugal 4–1 away in Portugal's first match since Cristiano Ronaldo retired from international football
stories.what: Denmark beat Portugal 4–1 away in UEFA Nations League Group A4, ending Portugal's four-match winning streak; Rasmus Højlund scored twice, Anadolu reported. It was Portugal's first match since Cristiano Ronaldo retired from international football.
stories.why: Ronaldo's retirement marks the end of an era for Portuguese football.
